whatTheyArgued: Warren & Brandeis, 'The Right to Privacy', Harvard Law Review 4 (1890), read on disk (Gutenberg 37368): new inventions (instantaneous photographs, newspapers) call for protecting the person, 'securing to the individual what Judge Cooley calls the right to be let alone' (the snip; the phrase is credited to Cooley and footnoted to Cooley on Torts). They argue the protection of thoughts, sentiments and emotions against publication is an instance of a more general right of the individual to be let alone, grounded not in private property but in an inviolate personality, and they list limits: the right does not bar publication of matter of public or general interest, and similar exceptions. The Olmstead dissent (1928) is a separate text: the line 'the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men' belongs there. It could not be sourced on disk (the archive.org item for Olmstead is a web-capture archive with no text file), so that quotation is unverified here.

scholarship.ref: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Privacy' (read via fetch, summary)
scholarship.supports: Warren & Brandeis present privacy as protecting an 'inviolate personality' against technology and press intrusion; Prosser later split the tort into four interests
scholarship.disputes: Thomson (1975) argues privacy reduces to other rights, against treating it as one right; scholars dispute whether W&B ground privacy in property or in personal inviolability (the text itself rejects the property reading).

scholarship.ref: Search-result summary on Cooley as source of the phrase and its path to Brandeis's Olmstead dissent (not read in full); confirmed independently in the 1890 text itself (credit to Cooley, footnote 10)
scholarship.supports: the phrase originates with Cooley (Treatise on Torts), later used by Brandeis in Olmstead

ourUse: privacy.js: a heuristic lint over code for data-sovereignty weak signals (raw key in localStorage, weak KDF, hardcoded secret, sensitive data to a remote sink), plus a 'sovereigntyHint' that leans code tasks toward E2EE, local-first, zero-knowledge and minimization; its instruments are UDHR Art. 12, EU Charter Art. 8, Convention 108+ and CARE/OCAP. The archon name credits Brandeis as the definer of privacy as 'the right to be let alone'.

bends.ours: privacy.js header: Brandeis's paper 'defined privacy as the right to be let alone'; compendium: Warren and Brandeis 'naming the right to be let alone'.
bends.theirs: The 1890 text attributes the phrase to Judge Cooley. W&B's contribution is arguing that it grounds a general legal right of privacy; they did not coin it.

bends.ours: Credit line quotes 'the right to be let alone - the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men' and dates it '(1890; 1928)'.
bends.theirs: The 'most comprehensive of rights' words do not appear in the 1890 article (searched). They are from the 1928 Olmstead dissent only. I could not verify the 1928 wording from a text on disk.

bends.ours: Applied to static analysis of source code for weak KDFs, key storage, and E2EE/local-first design.
bends.theirs: The 1890 article concerns publication by the press and photography and the common-law tort remedy; the dissent concerns wiretapping and the Fourth and Fifth Amendments. Neither addresses cryptography or software design.

bends.ours: Brandeis is made archon of 'data sovereignty', alongside CARE/OCAP and Convention 108+.
bends.theirs: W&B argue an individual's right against intrusion and publication, with express exceptions for public interest. Sovereignty over data, especially collective or jurisdictional (CARE/OCAP), is a different concept the instruments bring, not the source.

bends.ours: Compendium work ends 'The boundary is the person's own.'
bends.theirs: That sentence is ours, in the author-credit paragraph. W&B also qualify the right (public-interest exception), which the sentence omits.
